Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Hussein Shegow Mohamed Sunday November 8, 2026 After more than three decades, the United Nations political mission in Somalia closes today. The country asked for it. The harder question is whether its institutions are ready. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) concludes its mandate on 31 October 2026. On October 31, 2026, the UN ends its political mission in Somalia. A ceremony was held in Mogadishu earlier that week to commemorate the conclusion of 13 years of work that began with the creation of UNSOM in 2013. If you go back a little further, the story is older. In 1995, a political office was established by the UN for Somalia. Thus, it is not the end of a single mission when the doors close. It's the end of a long-standing habit. People are already asking what happens now. It's a fair question, and I don't think the honest answer is either "everything will be fine" or "the country will fall apart." advertisements Let's begin with something that is frequently overlooked. This was requested by Somalia. The foreign minister requested in a letter to the Security Council in May 2024 that the mission's mandate expire in October of that same year. Later, Mogadishu consented to a more gradual departure, and the Council unanimously approved a two-year transition that would conclude on October 31, 2026, with the mission being renamed UNTMIS. Its responsibilities were supposed to be transferred to Somali institutions and the remaining UN agencies. And they do remain. After the mandate expires, the UN has stated that it will continue to support Somalia. Humanitarian organizations, development initiatives, clinic staff, and food distributors all continue to exist. The political office, which consisted of a small team of advisors and diplomats tasked with reaching out to all parties, negotiating agreements, and documenting issues, disappears. That final point, in my opinion, is more important than we realize. Anyone who has followed Somali politics is aware of how frequently the real struggle is not with Al-Shabaab but rather between Mogadishu and the federal member states over issues like elections, the constitution, and power. Someone had to sit in the middle and be trusted by both parties when those discussions broke down in the past. Although it wasn't flawless, the UN was typically trusted enough to bring people together. Now, who does that? The Union of Africa? adjacent governments? The Gulf states, Turkey? Everyone in the room is aware of their shared interests in Somalia. An exit works when local institutions are already strong enough to carry the load, and it hurts when the exit date arrives before they are. Lessons from Liberia Examining another nation that experienced a similar situation is beneficial. I keep thinking about Liberia as an example. After fifteen years, UNMIL, the UN peacekeeping force stationed there, came to an end in March 2018. Liberia had recently accomplished something that many had doubted it could: in 2017, a president peacefully transferred power to a successor through an election, something that hadn't happened in decades. The exit was hailed as evidence of the nation's maturity. And it had, in certain respects. However, the institutions that were meant to keep things together proved to be weaker than the festivities suggested as Liberia battled complaints of corruption, growing costs, and street demonstrations in the years that followed. It is crucial to note that the nation did not return to war. However, the blue helmets' departure did not end the quiet process of reestablishing trust. Here, I should exercise caution. The closure in Somalia is a political mission, and UNMIL was a peacekeeping force with soldiers and police; the two are not the same. Liberia did not have an ongoing insurgency in 2018, but Somalia does. The lesson is still applicable, though. Three things to watch So where does Somalia stand? I'd say there are three things worth watching. The first is the election. The entire transition will appear to be successful if the major players agree to move on to the next round. We will soon learn the practical consequences of the UN's absence if it results in a disagreement over the regulations. The second is rights to humanity. In order to document abuses and speak out, journalists, activists, and displaced families depended on the mission. The government claims that national organizations can take over, and perhaps they can, but only if they are granted autonomy. It is not much of a commission if it is unable to hold the funders accountable. Thirdly, there is security. Al-Shabaab has not disappeared, and the African Union has not yet completed the transfer of security responsibilities. Weakness in the military and political disputes feed each other. Every time leaders engage in combat, the rebels gain ground. A test of ownership This does not imply that the choice was incorrect. A nation cannot continue to be governed by foreign powers indefinitely, and many Somalis were fed up with the idea that foreign powers controlled their politics. It makes sense to want to control your own destiny. Owning it, however, entails doing the difficult part, which entails making concessions, putting up with regulations that occasionally work against you, and creating institutions that outlive any one president. The UN is no longer involved in politics. We won't know for a few years whether that was courageous or premature. We do know that if the negotiations fail, no one else will be held accountable going forward. __________________________ Hussein Shegow Mohamed is a Somali writer and political and security analyst. He holds a Master’s degree in International Relations and Diplomacy and a Bachelor’s degree in International Relations. His work focuses on Somalia’s security, governance, and sustainable peace. somalia.content: Somalia’s Constitutional Test: Presidential power must answer to law - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Somalia’s Constitutional Test: Presidential power must answer to law Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Hirsi Abdulkadir Mohamed Sunday November 8, 2026 A constitutional limit means little if a president can respond to judicial scrutiny by replacing the leadership of the court examining his authority. That is the principle at stake in Somalia’s confrontation between the presidency and the judiciary. On 7 November 2026, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud attended the swearing-in of Ibrahim Idle Suleiman as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. He emphasized judicial independence, accountability and equal justice. Yet the circumstances surrounding the appointment raise a fundamental question: will the presidency accept those principles when they constrain its own power? Two days earlier, the Supreme Court reportedly ruled that the mandates of Somalia’s federal institutions had expired. It held that constitutional amendments increasing terms from four to five years did not automatically grant existing officeholders another year. The court directed political stakeholders to agree on an electoral framework within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, while limiting the government to routine administration. advertisements The dispute concerns more than the timing of an election. It tests whether Somalia’s constitutional institutions can impose meaningful limits on those who govern. Under Articles 60 and 91 of the 2012 Provisional Constitution, parliamentary and presidential terms were four years. Any claim to an additional year therefore depends on the legal effect of subsequent amendments, particularly their transitional provisions. Changing the length of future terms and extending an incumbent’s mandate are distinct legal acts. The latter requires a clear constitutional foundation because it changes the conditions under which authority was originally entrusted. Without that distinction, constitutional reform risks becoming a mechanism through which officeholders prolong their own rule. The ambition to introduce direct elections does not remove this obligation. Electoral reform must proceed through lawful institutions and procedures. Its democratic promise cannot, by itself, authorize an extension of power. The judicial leadership dispute makes the situation more serious. President Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed before the mandate ruling, citing concerns about the administration of justice. The Supreme Court subsequently declared the dismissal unconstitutional and accused the president of interfering with a pending constitutional case. The replacement’s swearing-in nevertheless proceeded. This sequence raises substantial concerns about executive interference, although timing alone does not establish personal motives. The presidency must explain the legal basis for removing the previous Chief Justice and appointing his successor while its own mandate is under judicial examination. Article 90(j) of the 2012 constitutional text connects presidential judicial appointments to recommendations from the Judicial Service Commission. Article 111A assigns that commission responsibilities concerning judicial recruitment and dismissal. The government should publish the relevant decrees and demonstrate compliance with the applicable framework, including any subsequent legal changes. A swearing-in ceremony cannot cure an appointment made without lawful authority. Nor does replacing a Chief Justice reverse an existing judgment. Any challenge to the court’s decision must follow an authorized legal process. The judiciary must also establish the basis of its authority. The 2012 constitutional framework assigns important constitutional functions to a distinct Constitutional Court. A complete assessment must therefore explain how the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Division acquired jurisdiction over this dispute, including through any applicable transitional legislation. The authenticated judgment, operative constitutional amendments and relevant judicial laws should be publicly accessible. Questions about jurisdiction or procedure deserve reasoned answers through lawful channels. They cannot simply become a justification for executive disregard. Meanwhile, Somalia must preserve essential public administration. Salaries, services and security responsibilities cannot be suspended while political leaders contest their mandates. But administrative continuity does not automatically preserve unrestricted presidential powers. If the reported caretaker limitations are legally effective, a consequential judicial appointment requires a specific legal justification. International partners should support transparency, judicial independence and an inclusive electoral settlement with clear deadlines. Their pursuit of stability must reinforce constitutional accountability. Accepting indefinite uncertainty over mandates would weaken the institutions on which lasting stability depends. Federal authorities, Federal Member States and opposition leaders must negotiate a credible electoral process while protecting peaceful political participation and the judiciary’s freedom to act. Political agreement can facilitate a lawful transition; it cannot permanently replace constitutional authority. President Mohamud has called for judicial independence. He should demonstrate that commitment by submitting his administration’s claimed mandate and judicial appointments to transparent legal scrutiny. The Constitution must bind the presidency when compliance carries a political cost. Otherwise, Somalia risks establishing a dangerous precedent: that those entrusted with power may decide for themselves when its limits apply. _________________________________ Hirsi Abdulkadir Mohamed is a lawyer and Horn of Africa political analyst. Photo courtesy of Egyptian Foreign Ministry. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty discussed Red Sea security and regional stability with his Somali and Djiboutian counterparts on Saturday, stressing that responsibility for the strategic waterway’s security and governance rests exclusively with countries bordering it. Abdelatty held separate meetings with Somali Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali and Djiboutian Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Hussein Omar on the sidelines of the 22nd Ordinary Session of the Executive Council of the Community of Sahel-Saharan States (CEN-SAD) in Tripoli, Libya. advertisements During his meeting with Abdi Ali, Abdelatty discussed ways to strengthen bilateral relations and expand cooperation, particularly in the economic, development and investment sectors. He reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to supporting efforts to build Somali state institutions and enhance their capabilities, reiterating Cairo’s firm support for Somalia’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the preservation of its national institutions. Abdelatty also reiterated Egypt’s categorical rejection of any unilateral measures that could undermine Somalia’s territorial integrity or infringe on its sovereignty. The two ministers exchanged views on developments in the Horn of Africa, highlighting the importance of strengthening national institutions and preserving the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries across the region. They also agreed to continue coordination and build on the outcomes of the consultative summit hosted by Egypt in El-Alamein in October, as part of broader efforts to promote peace, stability and development in the region. In his meeting with Djiboutian Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Hussein Omar, Abdelatty welcomed the two countries’ commitment to expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in the political, economic and investment fields. Their discussions covered cooperation in energy, logistics, ports, maritime connectivity and infrastructure, as well as ways to increase trade and mutual investment. Abdelatty also highlighted the importance of technical cooperation and capacity-building programmes delivered by Egyptian institutions. On regional developments, the two ministers exchanged views on the latest political and security developments in the Horn of Africa, particularly in Sudan and Somalia, and efforts to promote regional peace and stability. Abdelatty underscored the importance of supporting national institutions and safeguarding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries in the region. The pavilion was inaugurated by Somalia’s Minister of Commerce and Industry, Jama Mohamed Hassan, alongside Somalia’s Ambassador to China, Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi, during the ninth edition of the international trade exhibition. advertisements The ceremony was attended by senior Somali government officials, representatives of the Somali Chamber of Commerce and Industry, business leaders and members of the Somali delegation. Somali companies are displaying products including sesame seeds, frankincense and myrrh, while promoting investment opportunities in livestock, fisheries and mineral resources. The government hopes the exhibition will help Somali producers establish direct connections with Chinese importers, identify market requirements and secure new commercial partnerships. The expo, held at Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center from Nov. 5 to 10, has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors and participants from 162 countries, regions and international organizations, according to organizers. Somalia is among the countries participating in the expo’s national exhibition for the first time, providing a platform to introduce its products and investment potential to international buyers. The exhibition also provides an opportunity to attract investment in local production, processing and packaging, which could enable Somali businesses to export more finished products rather than relying primarily on raw materials. “The Embassy of Somalia in China views this participation as a significant starting point for expanding the country’s exports and creating new markets that will benefit Somali farmers, livestock herders, fishers, and businesspeople,” the embassy said. The embassy credited the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the Office of the Prime Minister, other government institutions and Somali entrepreneurs for coordinating the country's participation. It also praised Somali businesspeople based in China and those who traveled from Somalia for presenting products and investment opportunities at the pavilion. The embassy said it would continue facilitating connections between Somali and Chinese businesses and following up on commercial opportunities identified during the exhibition. Somalia’s participation comes as the government seeks to diversify export markets, attract foreign investment and strengthen the country's domestic production capacity. Targeting international partners, the council underscored the court’s timeline: parliament’s mandate expired April 14, 2026, and the presidential term ended May 15, 2026. As a result, the council declared all contracts, policy decisions, and legislative agreements enacted after those dates null and void, pledging a full review once legal supremacy is re-established. somalia.content: A Partnership Under Strain: U.S. Reaffirms Support While Defunding the Mission Somalia Depends On - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Nationwide A Partnership Under Strain: U.S. Reaffirms Support While Defunding the Mission Somalia Depends On November 8, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi met with the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires, Ruth Anne Stevens-Klitz, on Sunday to discuss the future of the AUSSOM mission and the handover of a former AU base in Barawe to the Somali National Army, as Washington simultaneously reaffirms its security partnership and withdraws the funding that sustains the mission. According to a statement from the Ministry of Defence, the meeting focused on strengthening the strategic partnership between Somalia and the United States in defence and security, and on ongoing operations against the Khawaarij. The two sides specifically discussed the mandate and future of AUSSOM, emphasizing the importance of ensuring that the security transition is well-planned, coordinated, and based on the capabilities and readiness of the Somali National Armed Forces. The meeting also addressed the handover of a former AUSSOM military base in Barawe, which has now been taken over by the Somali National Army. The ministry described the handover as part of broader efforts to bolster the capacity of the national forces and to assume full responsibility for the country’s security. A Partnership Under Strain The Barawe handover is not an isolated event. It comes as Uganda withdraws its bilateral troops from the same region, and as AUSSOM prepares to take over positions that Ugandan forces are vacating. The Somali army commander, Brigadier General Ibrahim Mohamed Mohamud, visited Barawe last week to instruct troops to remain on high alert and intensify operations against Al-Shabaab , but the military statement did not clarify whether Somali forces would take over the AU bases being left behind. The broader context is one of a security architecture unravelling under financial pressure. The United States notified the African Union in July 2026 that it would end funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), which provides food, fuel, water, medical support, and casualty evacuation for AUSSOM’s roughly 12,000 personnel, as FTL Somalia reported on the U.S. decision to end UNSOS support . The UN support office has already begun preparing for liquidation, issuing a public tender to sell generators, medical equipment, and heavy machinery valued at approximately $30 million, as the unravelling security architecture has been documented. Washington has cited frustration with the Somali government’s failure to take full ownership of its security functions and sustain progress against Al-Shabaab. Yet the same U.S. officials who are withdrawing logistical support continue to engage with Somali security leadership on training and capacity-building. Stevens-Klitz’s meeting with Fiqi is a reaffirmation of a partnership that is simultaneously being defunded. As the Somali army chief’s earlier meeting with Stevens-Klitz demonstrated, military-to-military cooperation continues even as the financial foundations of the mission erode. The Barawe Handover and the Capability Question The handover of the Barawe base is a concrete step in the transition that AUSSOM’s mandate envisions. But it is also a test of whether the Somali National Army can hold territory that foreign forces have secured. Barawe was captured from Al-Shabaab in 2014, and the militants had used its port to bring in fighters and weapons and to export charcoal. Losing it would be a significant setback. As joint SNA and AUSSOM patrols in Barawe have shown, the transition from AU-led to Somali-led security in the region is already underway. The Somali forces taking over the base face the same constraints that have plagued the SNA across the country: limited logistics, payroll irregularities, and command-and-control weaknesses. Farhan Isak Yusuf, deputy executive director of Somali Public Agenda, warned that the Somali army lacks resources and faces a difficult security environment in Lower Shabelle, the region where the Ugandan troops were stationed and which is critical to protecting Mogadishu. Fiqi’s statement emphasized the government’s commitment to building a professional and capable national army, one fully equipped to fulfill its constitutional mandate. He expressed gratitude to the United States for its sustained support. But the gratitude is directed at a partner whose support is becoming more conditional and more limited, even as the security challenges mount. The return of the 22nd Gorgor Brigade from advanced training in Türkiye is a reminder that Somalia’s security partnerships extend beyond Washington, but the Gorgor brigades are a small elite force and cannot fill every gap left by departing AU troops. Critical Note The meeting between Fiqi and Stevens-Klitz takes place at a moment of profound contradiction in U.S.-Somalia security relations. Washington is simultaneously reaffirming its commitment to the Somali National Army and withdrawing the funding that sustains the AU mission the SNA depends on. The United States wants to help Somalia build its own forces while reducing its financial exposure to the broader security architecture. That is not an irrational policy. It reflects a legitimate frustration with the pace of progress and a reasonable expectation that Somalia should take increasing responsibility for its own security. But it is a policy that is being implemented in the middle of a political crisis, as the Supreme Court has declared the President’s mandate expired and the government’s authority is contested. The SNA is being asked to assume greater responsibility at the exact moment when the government that commands it is least able to provide the resources and direction it needs. The Barawe handover is a symbol of the transition. It is also a warning. A base handed over without the logistics to sustain it, without the payroll to pay the soldiers who hold it, and without the political consensus to legitimize the authority they represent is not a secure base. It is a position waiting to be tested. Al-Shabaab is preparing to exploit any vacuum left by departing foreign troops. The question is whether the Somali forces taking over Barawe are ready for that test, or whether the handover is a ceremony that precedes a retreat. South West State President Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe arrived in Jowhar and was welcomed by Guudlaawe at Mohamed Dheere Airport, thanking him for attending the ceremony. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud is also expected in Jowhar, where he will inaugurate the reconstructed Jowhar Airport before attending the swearing-in, alongside other federal and regional officials and diplomats. The JSP Consolidation The inauguration follows Guudlaawe’s re-election on October 24, in which he secured 81 votes in the regional parliament, defeating Nur Ilmi Halane of the Ramaas party, as FTL Somalia reported on the parliamentary ballot . The Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP) holds 78 of the 99 seats in the regional assembly, giving Guudlaawe a commanding majority in a chamber that the ruling party dominates. This is the second federal member state inauguration in less than a week. As FTL Somalia reported on the Galmudug ceremony , Liibaan Ahmed Hassan was inaugurated in Dhusamareb on Thursday after the JSP secured a similar dominant majority in the Galmudug parliament. The pattern is now clear: Galmudug, Hirshabelle, and South West State are all under the effective control of the JSP and the federal government that backs it, while Puntland and Jubaland remain outside the fold and reject the federal electoral process entirely. The JSP’s regional strategy, backed by President Mohamud, has produced a string of victories in federal member state contests. As the September 30 direct elections demonstrated , the party won 158 of 222 local council seats and 78 of 99 House of the People seats in Hirshabelle, a landslide that set the stage for Guudlaawe’s return. But the parliamentary arithmetic that secured his re-election has not resolved the political dispute that has been building in Hiiraan since the JSP renominated him. The Hawadle Revolt The Hawadle community, dominant in Hiiraan, has rejected Guudlaawe’s re-election and the JSP’s power-sharing arrangement. As FTL Somalia reported when the dispute first escalated , Hawadle elders and politicians declared that any election held without a prior political agreement would be unacceptable, warning of unrest and holding the electoral committee responsible for the consequences. The dispute dates back to Hirshabelle’s formation in 2016, when an informal agreement allocated the presidency to the Hawadle, but the JSP’s renomination of Guudlaawe, an Abgaal from Middle Shabelle, deepened the grievance. The selection of Abdifatah Hassan Afrah, a former Hiiraan governor, as vice president was intended to balance the ticket, but it did not satisfy the Hawadle demand for the presidency itself. The situation escalated dramatically over the weekend. As FTL Somalia reported on the mobilization , Hawadle clan leader Ugaas Yusuf called for mass armed mobilization in Beledweyne, urging residents and security personnel from Hiiraan to prepare to defend the region against what he described as a planned federal government attack. Hundreds of residents reportedly mobilized with weapons, and there were unconfirmed reports that soldiers of Hawadle origin were defecting from the Somali National Army to join the standoff. Former Hirshabelle Parliament Speaker Osman Barre Mohamed backed the Ugaas and warned that a military offensive against Hiiraan would “lead to the collapse of the government itself.” Federal troops reportedly gathered at the Ugaas’s residence in Beledweyne on Saturday, and security personnel linked to NISA and local Macawisley militia remained in a standoff near the residence where Vice President Afrah was staying. The former NISA director, Abdullahi Mohamed Ali Sanbaloolshe, has returned to Beledweyne with an armed convoy and is positioning himself as the political leader of a movement seeking an independent administration for Hiiraan, as FTL Somalia reported on his arrival and the unravelling of Hirshabelle’s authority . Sanbaloolshe has backed calls for a separate Hiiraan administration and has not ruled out cooperation with Al-Shabaab . The mobilization also has implications for the fight against Al-Shabaab. The Macawisley fighters who have been drawn into the political dispute were among the most effective local forces in Hiiraan, and their withdrawal from the frontlines against the militants creates an opening that the group is likely to exploit. As FTL Somalia reported on the Hawadle-Al-Shabaab dynamic , the community’s sense of abandonment by the federal government has already pushed some of its leaders toward local agreements with the militants. Critical Note Guudlaawe’s inauguration is a victory for the JSP’s regional strategy. The party now controls Galmudug, Hirshabelle, and South West State, and it has done so with the federal government’s backing and the international community’s attendance. The parliamentary arithmetic is decisive, and the ceremony in Jowhar will project an image of normalcy and consolidation. But the image is misleading. A president elected by a chamber his party dominates, in a vote that the Hawadle leadership rejected as a sham, is not a president whose authority extends across the territory he claims to govern. As the outgoing Hawadle Vice President Yusuf Ahmed Hagar Dabageed said before the vote, “any result from that sham does not apply to Hiiraan.” The JSP has won the vote in Jowhar. It has not won the acceptance of Hiiraan. The armed mobilization in Beledweyne, the defections, and the standoff at the Vice President’s residence are not peripheral disturbances. They are the consequence of a political strategy that prioritized parliamentary control over consensus-building. The federal government’s role in this is central. President Mohamud backed Guudlaawe’s renomination, and the JSP’s dominance in regional assemblies is a product of federal influence as much as local popularity. The inauguration in Jowhar will be a celebration for the JSP and its allies. It will not be a resolution of the crisis in Hiiraan. The Hawadle leadership has chosen to mobilize rather than accept the outcome, and the federal government has chosen to back the JSP rather than mediate. The consequences of those choices will play out in Beledweyne, not in Jowhar, and they will not be resolved by a ceremony. الجديان" في العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، بعد غيابهم عن الحصة التدريبية الأولى التي اقتصرت على المحترفين في الخارج واللاعبين الشباب الجدد في قائمة المدرب كواسي أبياه. ويسيطر نجوم العملاقين على قائمة مدرب السودان بوجود 19 لاعبًا يمثلون القوام الأساسي للمنتخب، في مشهد طبيعي لاستمرار الفريقين بالمنافسات المحلية والقارية، وكان المدرب قد منح الفرصة للاعبي الفريقين للمشاركة في مبارياتهما مؤخرًا بالدوري
